quiz.q: A DataWeave global variable is declared with `var` in the header of a Transform Message. Where can it be used?
options: Anywhere in the Mule event, like Set Variable
Throughout that script only — not outside that Transform Message
In every flow of the project
quiz.explain: A DWL global variable covers the whole script but isn't accessible outside that Transform Message; Set Variable, target variables etc. live on the Mule event.

quiz.q: A date arrives in JSON and `as Date {format: ...}` on it doesn't work. Why?
options: JSON dates arrive as strings — first convert the string to a Date in its current format, then format it
quiz.explain: This confuses most people: parse the string with its current format first, then reformat the Date.

quiz.q: You need to convert an object into an array of its values. Which function?
quiz.explain: pluck: object → array. reduce: array → object. mapObject outputs an object.

quiz.q: In `mapObject`, what do `$`, `$$` and `$$$` refer to?
quiz.explain: Count the lambda parameters `(value, key, index)` in order. For `map`, `$` = item and `$$` = index.

quiz.q: How do you stop null fields from appearing in the DataWeave output?
quiz.explain: skipNullOn goes on the output line, above `---`; values are attributes, elements or everywhere.

quiz.q: In the API-led architecture, which layer applies the business logic?
quiz.explain: System fetches data with no business logic; process applies it; experience is a wrapper with the non-functional policies.

quiz.q: Three systems and two consumers that need different data. What is the minimum number of APIs?
quiz.explain: 3 system + 1 process + 2 experience = 6; it would be 5 if one experience API served both consumers.

quiz.q: Request size grows from 10 KB to 25–40 KB. Which scaling fits?
options: Vertical — increase the worker's vCore size
quiz.explain: Vertical scaling for larger payloads; horizontal (more workers) for more requests and high availability.

quiz.q: Which set of CloudHub worker numbers is correct?
options: 2 apps per worker; 0.2–8 vCores; max 16 workers
1 app per worker; 0.1–16 vCores; max 8 workers for one app
10 apps per worker; 1–10 vCores; max 4 workers
1 app per worker; 0.1–8 vCores; unlimited workers
quiz.explain: Also: up to 10 apps per vCore, since the smallest worker is 0.1 vCore.

quiz.q: In the hybrid deployment model, who runs the control plane and the runtime plane?
options: MuleSoft runs the control plane; the client runs the runtime plane
The client runs the control plane; MuleSoft runs the runtime
quiz.explain: CloudHub: MuleSoft both; on-premise: client both; hybrid: apps on client servers managed with Anypoint Platform.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a cluster from a server group?
options: A server group has failover; a cluster doesn't
Cluster nodes are aware of each other, share state and fail over; server group instances are isolated and only simplify deployment
Clusters allow different Mule runtime versions
Server groups can only have 2 servers
quiz.explain: Both are single deployment targets, and all servers must run the same Mule runtime version. A cluster has up to 8 servers.

quiz.q: Requests exceed the shared load balancer's regional rate limit. What do consumers get?
quiz.explain: The SLB returns 503 (not 429) over its limit; a dedicated load balancer inside a VPC avoids the lower limit.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a keystore and a truststore?
options: A keystore holds trusted CA certificates; a truststore holds your private key
A keystore holds your private key and certificates that identify you; a truststore holds certificates you trust
A truststore is only used by servers
quiz.explain: When consuming HTTPS, the client checks the server's certificate against its truststore.

quiz.q: In two-way TLS (mTLS), what does the server need besides its keystore?
options: A truststore with the clients' public certificates
quiz.explain: In mutual authentication both sides verify each other, so the server's truststore holds the client public certificates.

quiz.q: What are the steps to consume an HTTPS service from Mule?
options: Generate a keystore and set it on the HTTP Listener
Configure HTTPS on the HTTP Request connector and set the truststore in its TLS section
quiz.explain: To expose HTTPS you put the keystore on the Listener's TLS section; to consume, the truststore on the Requester's.

cards.back: Sets a value when the payload or field is absent or null: `fullName: payload.name default "XYZ Bank"`.
In the header with `fun`: `fun myfunction(p1) = upper(p1)`, then call `myfunction("Hello")` → "HELLO".
Set Variable, target variable on components, Transform Message (output to a variable), Scripting — all Mule event scope. DW global `var` (that script only) and DW local (`using`, its scope only).
`.key` single, `.*key` multi (one level), `..key` descendants, `[i]` index (`[-1]` last), `[0 to 2]` range, `.@attr` attribute, `.@` all attributes.
`now()`, `now() >> "IST"` (time zone), `as Date {format: "yyyy-MMM-dd"}`, `now() + |PT15M|` (time), `now() + |P10D|` (date), `.year/.month/.day`.
**PT** = hours, minutes, seconds; **P** = years, months, days. Written between pipes in capitals; use `-` to subtract.
Both iterate over an object; pluck outputs the values into an **array**, mapObject outputs an **object**.
map: `$` = item, `$$` = index (array → array). mapObject: `$` = value, `$$` = key, `$$$` = index (object → object).
`output application/json skipNullOn = "everywhere"` (or attributes / elements).
`p('propertyname')`; secure: `p('secure::propertyname')`.
joinBy: array → string with a separator (`["a","b","c"] joinBy "-"` → "a-b-c"). splitBy: string → array.
`isEmpty()` works on array, object or string. Mask: `payload mask field("age") with "***"`.
Get the application and flow name — in Mule 4 they work only in the Logger.
Reads a URL or file and returns its content — e.g. `readUrl("classpath://file.json", "application/json")`; used by MUnit-recorded files in src/test/resources.
**System**: connects to systems, no business logic. **Process**: business logic. **Experience**: wrapper exposed to clients, with all non-functional policies.

cards.front: Why more than one experience API?
cards.back: Only when consumers need different data or policies (e.g. mobile needs less than web, or a third party needs an extra policy).
Pros: reusability, a break affects limited functionality, faster time to market in the long run, easy to maintain. Cons: more initial time, more vCores → more cost.
99% via the HTTP Request connector; alternatively publish an API to Exchange as a connector.
Design → Implementation → Testing → Deploy → Monitor.
An Anypoint Platform module to deploy and manage Mule apps on CloudHub, on-premise or RTF: deploy/undeploy, stop/restart, change runtime version, worker size, check logs, scale.
A unit of compute capacity on CloudHub; max 10 apps per vCore (0.1 vCore each).
Capacity (by vCores), isolation (separate container), manageability (independent), locality (a specific region).
Horizontal: more workers — more requests, high availability. Vertical: bigger vCore size — larger payloads (or more requests).
A runtime engine to host and run Mule apps, like an application server; on-premises or in the cloud; can host several apps.
Runtime Fabric — container-based (Kubernetes and Docker) deployment and orchestration on the client's premises or cloud.
Control plane: Design Center, Exchange, Management Center (design, deploy, manage). Runtime plane: Mule runtime, connectors, supporting services.

CloudHub: MuleSoft runs both planes, max 10 apps/vCore, no domain project, less maintenance, Anypoint MQ available. On-premise: client runs both, more apps/vCore, domain project, more maintenance, more data control.
Up to 8 servers acting as one deployment target and HA unit; nodes are aware of each other, share info, and fail over.

cards.front: How is clustering achieved on CloudHub?
cards.back: Deploy to 2+ workers — they're spread across data centers and the load balancer distributes requests round robin.
Implementation URL: generated by CloudHub on deploy. Proxy URL: of a proxy on top of the API, where policies are applied.
VPC: a dedicated, isolated cloud space inside CloudHub (extra cost). VPN: a secure connection between the MuleSoft VPC and the on-premise network.
SLB: default, shared per region, 8081/8082, no custom certs, lower rate limit → 503. DLB: optional within a VPC, 8091/8092, custom certs, single domain, two-way auth.
A common project holding shared property files and connector configs for multiple apps — on-premise only.
JAR → Runtime Manager; deploy from Studio; CI/CD pipeline (Jenkins); drop the JAR into an on-premise runtime (an `.anchor` file appears on success).
Possible — then only system logs remain in Runtime Manager; app logs go to an external service like Splunk. CloudHub keeps about 100 MB.
Both are cryptographic protocols. SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) is the old one; TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the improved, more secure version used today.
One-way: only the client verifies the server (client truststore holds the server certificate). Two-way (mTLS): both verify — each side has a keystore and a truststore.

cards.front: Steps to expose an API as HTTPS
cards.back: Generate a keystore (`keytool -genkey`), set the HTTP Listener protocol to HTTPS, and configure the keystore in its TLS section.
Symmetric: one shared secret key. Asymmetric (public-key): a key pair — more secure.
Signed by the developer/company, not a public CA — fine for agreed internal use, unsafe for public apps.
